title: Every mutation appends a full copy of the doc-section FTS index; stores grow without bound
body:
**THE STORE GROWS WITHOUT BOUND IN PROPORTION TO HOW OFTEN A PROJECT HAS BEEN WRITTEN TO, NOT TO HOW MUCH IT HOLDS.** Two independent mechanisms, both fixed. **The mechanism this issue was originally filed with was wrong, and both corrections are recorded below rather than overwritten** -- a filing whose premise is wrong sends the next reader down the same path.

## What the original filing got wrong

It said `Store::write_doc_sections`'s `DELETE FROM doc_sections` never runs, on the evidence that rowids stay contiguous `1..N`. **The `DELETE` runs and is fine.** Contiguous rowids are equally consistent with a working delete: FTS5 keeps its content in an ordinary rowid table, so after a wholesale delete the next insert starts at 1 again. The evidence never discriminated between the two hypotheses it was offered as proof of.

It also nominated the FTS5 idiom `INSERT INTO doc_sections(doc_sections) VALUES('delete-all')` as the obvious fix. **SQLite refuses it on this table** -- _"'delete-all' may only be used with a contentless or external content fts5 table"_ -- so it would have failed at runtime. `'rebuild'` is the idiom that applies here.

## Mechanism 1: three derivations of the prose index, disagreeing

The index was derived in three places and no two agreed. `ingest::read` derived every kind and was correct. The restore path in `facade.rs` dropped `thread` and `work-package` sections before re-deriving them, and was correct. **The mutation path dropped only `work-package`.**

`ingest::collect_wp_text` emits three kinds of section and its name names one: a thread's own objective and context, one per text attachment, and one per work package. The first two carry `owner_type: "thread"`, so the mutation path kept them from canon AND re-derived them -- **one extra copy of every thread-owned section on every mutation, for the life of the store.** A filter written against that function's name rather than its body was a reasonable mistake to make, which is why the name moved too.

**The same path never derived issue prose at all.** Nothing outside `ingest::read` split an issue body, so a body written by `issues add --body` sat in the model, rendered everywhere a human looks, and reached the FTS index only at the next full ingest. That is AC-06.4's failure shape -- an unpopulated index answers byte-identically to a genuine miss -- and it is the same defect in the opposite direction: threads over-indexed, issues under-indexed, one code block, one cause.

**Fix:** `ingest::sections_of(project, threads, issues)` is now the only derivation, and all three callers use it. It replaces the whole index from the whole model, so there is no set to name and nothing to drift. `collect_wp_text` is `collect_thread_prose`.

**Measured, rows against distinct `(file, owner_id, seq)`, before the fix:** Baize 1.0x (a store with no mutations since it was built -- the control that makes this a defect rather than a schema artefact), Conflab 5.9x, Intent 8.9x, Lamplight 13.1x, Laksa 56.6x. Only `owner_type = thread` duplicated; work-packages and issues were 1.0x throughout, which is the signature the mechanism above predicts exactly.

## Mechanism 2: the inverted index is tombstoned, never truncated -- and this is where the gigabytes are

`doc_sections` is written one way only: emptied and refilled. **`DELETE FROM` an FTS5 table does not remove the deleted rows' terms from the inverted index; it writes a delete marker for each of them into `doc_sections_data`.** Under this write pattern the markers accumulate on every mutation, for the life of the store.

**Nothing reports it.** The row count is correct, the content table is the right size, searches keep answering correctly, and `VACUUM` reclaims none of it because tombstones are live data rather than free pages.

Measured on Laksa **after mechanism 1's duplicate rows were already repaired**: 859 sections holding 5 MB of content, against **589 MB of `doc_sections_data`**.

**Fix:** `write_doc_sections` follows its `DELETE` with `INSERT INTO doc_sections(doc_sections) VALUES('rebuild')`. The content table is empty at that instant, so the rebuild costs nothing and truncates what it replaces.

## Existing stores: one ordinary sync repairs them, and a vacuum is a separate question

No migration or repair tooling is needed. On a copy of Laksa, one `intent sync --to-store` with the fixed binary:

| measure                | before  | after  |
| ---------------------- | ------: | -----: |
| `doc_sections` rows    |  48,524 |    859 |
| `doc_sections_data`    | 589 MB  |   1 MB |
| `intent st list`, warm | 1536 ms |  54 ms |
| `intent st list`, cold | 6807 ms |  54 ms |

**The file itself stays 2.3 GB, and that turns out not to matter for speed.** A subsequent `VACUUM` takes it to 14.8 MB and the same timings come back 54-60 ms -- unchanged. SQLite does not read free pages, so **reclaiming the file is a disk-space question and not a performance one**, and the two should not be bundled.

## Consequence, which is how this was found

**The symptom was hv reporting that `intent explore` is slow to start on a large project.** It is not large projects; it is heavily-written ones. Lamplight has three times Laksa's threads and a fifth of its duplication.

`export.rs` already recorded that "98.6% of a real store's bytes are `doc_sections_*`" -- that observation is this defect seen from the other side, read as a property of the data rather than as growth.

## Still not measured

- **Whether any other table duplicates or tombstones the same way.** Only `doc_sections` was examined, and only it is FTS5.
- **Whether the estate wants a maintenance verb that vacuums.** The measurement above says it would buy disk and not speed, so it is a judgement call rather than a follow-on defect.
